final_proof:
Let \(X=(E,*,g)\) be an object of \((\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\). By the definition of a comma category, \(E\) is an object of \(\mathbf C\) and
\[
g:\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(E)=E\longrightarrow F(*)=C.
\]
Thus \(g:E\to C\) is an object of the slice category \(\mathbf C/C\), so the stated object assignment of \(J\) is well-defined.

Now take a morphism
\[
(k,\operatorname{id}_*):(E,*,g)\longrightarrow(E',*,g')
\]
in the comma category. Its components satisfy \(k:E\to E'\) in \(\mathbf C\) and the comma-category compatibility equation
\[
F(\operatorname{id}_*)\circ g
 =g'\circ\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(k).
\]
Since \(F(\operatorname{id}_*)=\operatorname{id}_C\) and the identity functor sends \(k\) to \(k\), this equation reduces to
\[
g'\circ k=g.
\]
But a morphism from \(g:E\to C\) to \(g':E'\to C\) in the slice \(\mathbf C/C\) is precisely a morphism \(k:E\to E'\) satisfying \(g'\circ k=g\). Hence the stated assignment \(J(k,\operatorname{id}_*)=k\) is well-defined and has the required source and target.

It remains to verify the functor laws. The identity morphism of \((E,*,g)\) in the comma category is \((\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*)\). Therefore
\[
J(\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*)=\operatorname{id}_E,
\]
which is the identity morphism of the slice object \(g:E\to C\), since \(g\circ\operatorname{id}_E=g\). Thus \(J\) preserves identities.

Finally, suppose
\[
(k,\operatorname{id}_*):(E,*,g)\to(E',*,g')
\quad\text{and}\quad
(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*):(E',*,g')\to(E'',*,g'')
\]
are composable morphisms. Composition in a comma category is componentwise, so
\[
(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ(k,\operatorname{id}_*)
=(\ell\circ k,\operatorname{id}_*).
\]
Consequently,
\[
J\bigl((\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ(k,\operatorname{id}_*)\bigr)
=J(\ell\circ k,\operatorname{id}_*)
=\ell\circ k
=J(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ J(k,\operatorname{id}_*).
\]
Hence \(J\) preserves composition. Its object and morphism assignments are therefore well-defined and satisfy both functor axioms, so \(J:(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\to\mathbf C/C\) is a covariant functor.
